lei-y1-bast: Both develop academic information use, argument, reflection and collaboration. UCR combines these with personal development and civic engagement; Leiden’s assessed assignment addresses biomedical science and society.
lei-y1-human-biology: Both connect human anatomical structure with function. UCR emphasises regional and system anatomy, spatial reasoning, specimens and medical images; Leiden also introduces embryology and development.
lei-y1-biomolecules: Both introduce biological molecules, cells, membranes and their integrated functions. UCR provides broader molecular and cellular foundations rather than the same laboratory sequence.
lei-y1-r: Both use R for data handling, visualisation and reproducible analysis. UCR extends into text and spatial data and a data-based research project.
lei-y1-molecular-biology: Both study DNA replication and repair, gene expression, cell division and cell fate. UCR integrates cellular regulation and molecular therapeutic targets; Leiden includes its own developmental and experimental sequence.
lei-y1-research-methods: Both develop empirical questions, study design and statistical analysis. UCR practises survey and experimental research with R in social and behavioural contexts, while Leiden centres biomedical studies.
lei-y1-metabolism-b: Both develop integrated metabolic pathways, enzyme regulation and biomolecular transformations. UCR includes biochemical disease analysis; this does not cover both Leiden metabolism modules independently.
lei-y1-medical-genetics: Both connect inheritance, genetic variation, molecular diagnosis and disease. UCR combines genetics with cellular pathology, neoplasia and research-proposal design.
lei-y2-immunology: Both study innate and adaptive immune mechanisms, cellular interactions, immune disease and intervention. UCR also examines infection and flow-cytometry data; Leiden has a separate infection module.
lei-y2-design-analysis: Both develop study-design reasoning, regression, group comparisons, categorical outcomes and model checks. Leiden additionally specifies survival analysis and biomedical measurement validation; UCR applications centre health and behaviour.
lei-y2-neuroscience: Both concern nervous-system biology. UCR develops comparative brain anatomy, physiology, regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms; the relation is bounded by the available current Leiden module evidence.
lei-y2-reflection: Both use philosophical and ethical reasoning to examine difficult questions. UCR develops general moral theories and independent argument; Leiden specifically examines biomedical knowledge, scientific responsibility and research dilemmas.
lei-y2-physiology: Both examine cardiovascular, respiratory and renal functions, homeostasis and clinical illustrations. UCR covers the wider adult human body; it does not establish Leiden’s additional prerequisite rule.
lei-y2-hormones: Both connect neural mechanisms with behaviour, dysfunction and psychoactive drugs. UCR centres higher cognitive functions and experimental design; Leiden additionally integrates endocrine cascades, stress, reproduction and gene-expression analysis.
lei-y2-pathology: Both link organ function, disease mechanisms, symptoms, diagnostic findings and therapeutic intervention. UCR uses clinical cases and coherent pathophysiological reasoning; Leiden adds dedicated tissue pathology and anatomical practical work. External progression remains unresolved.
lei-y3-oncology: Both examine therapeutic targets and drug intervention. UCR supplies pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and antimicrobial/neural/immune applications; it does not reproduce the dedicated cancer mechanisms, tumour microenvironment and cancer-cell experiment.
